utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Good morning to all your present here in the court-room, the Prosecution, the Defence, as well as the accused who are all with us. Today we are going to hear a witness, but before we bring the witness in the court-room let me say that tomorrow at the beginning of the hearing we'll let you know how time will be divided, time left for the remainder of the cross-examination of the witness we had yesterday, and we will also tell you tomorrow how we think, how we believe that the witnesses for next week should be organised, considering that we will have two witnesses testifying under Rule 89(F) procedure. This is a procedure that has already been used in the Krajisnik case, but that it is not of very common use here at the Tribunal. The advantage of this procedure is that in the interest of justice we can speed up the hearing of some witnesses, and we'll let you know tomorrow what we've decided about the matter because the Judges will have a meeting this afternoon to deal with this issue. I'm going to ask the usher to bring the witness in and if it's all right, then the Prosecutor -- the representatives of the US government will sit behind Mr. Scott, if everybody agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. Thank you. I'll introduce, Your Honour, when they come in, if it's agreeable to the Court, I'll introduce the two representatives to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one brief matter, Mr. President, for scheduling purposes, can I assume that yesterday's witness will be next Monday? If it's -- if you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it should be the case, unless the Prosecutor has difficulties with the matter, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, again, Your Honour, we've asked yesterday for the Defence to provide us any additional information on cross-examination for next week. If they can, that would be very helpful to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Good morning, sir. You are a witness called by the Prosecution to testify in this case, the case of Prlic et al., but before I ask you to take the solemn declaration I would ask you to stand up. Very well. Can you please give me your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Peter Galbraith, born December 31st, 1950.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please tell me what are your current functions, occupation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an author -- author, writer, and I have a small consulting business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you ever testified before the Tribunal on the events that took place in various territories of the former Yugoslavia? If that's the case, if you've already testified, in what case have you testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've testified in two cases, in the Milosevic case and the Martic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you testified before other domestic courts, to testify about those matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to ask you to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated. Sir, let me give you some information before I give the floor to the representative of the Prosecution. You are a Prosecution witness, that's what I said earlier on. You will have to answer questions put to you by the Prosecution within the framework of the direct examination. The Prosecution envisages around four hours and a half for your direct examination. Once the Prosecution has completed the direct examination, the Defence that is represented by several Defence counsel, and each counsel will ask you questions on the behalf of the accused and some of the accused might ask you questions directly, but for the Defence we have planned or we have scheduled 315 minutes. We have to do such counting because we are pressed for time. The four Judges who are sitting before you can at any time take the floor and put questions to you. There is something a bit specific about your testimony because your government requested a number of protective measures that are provided for by the Rules. That's why we have here in the court-room two representatives of your government who are sitting behind the Prosecutor, and if the Prosecutor produces documents through -- as part of your testimony, some of these documents will be filed under seal. In other words, these documents will only be reviewed in private or closed session. Another specificity of your testimony is that as part of the cross-examination, that is common law, Anglo-Saxon procedure you're very familiar with, as part of the cross-examination, the Defence will not be able to ask you any question -- on any matter that has not been dealt with by the Prosecution. And we will make sure this rule is complied with. The representatives of your government may at any time, if they wish to do so, tell us that they object to a question put to you by the Defence. They can do so if they believe that Rule 70 has been infringed upon by the question put to you by the Defence. If such a case arises, then the Judges will have to rule. Furthermore, I would like to ask you to respond very precisely to the questions put to you, and if you encounter any difficulty please inform us immediately and we'll rule on this. For technical reasons, we have to take a break every one and a half hour, a 20-minute break in order to change the tapes. We'll therefore have two breaks today, and we'll complete our day's work today at quarter to 2.00. And tomorrow the hearing will start at 2.15. You will have the entire morning. And on Thursday, the hearing will start at 9.00. Thus, in any case your testimony will be completed on Thursday at a quarter to 2.00. Mr. Scott, can you please introduce the representatives of the American government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honour, Mr. President, Your Honours. I would be pleased to introduce the two representatives that are present in court this morning for the United States government. Seated behind me are Ms. Karen Johnson and Ms. Susan Aleksander, both of whom are lawyers for the United States State Department. Ms. Johnson is here from Washington, DC, and Ms. Aleksander works at the US embassy here in The Hague. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On behalf of all the Judges, I'd like to say good morning to them, including Ms. Johnson, who is from Washington. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, ambassador.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we've gotten your full name and date of birth in answers to questions from the President. Let me briefly touch on some of your educational background and some of your professional and vocational experiences. I understand, sir, that you received a bachelor's degree from Harvard university in 1973?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you received a master's degree from Oxford university in 1975?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I understand you have a law degree from Georgetown university which you received in 1990?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I also understand that from 1979 until approximately 1993 you were a senior advisor to the United States Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us just in a few sentences the nature of that work, the kind of things you were involved in.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: For most of the period I was responsible for the committees -- one of the committee's major pieces of legislation, the Foreign Relations Authorisation Act, which funded the state department and related agencies. I handled the near east and south Asia for the committee. And then for 1991 until I left on June 24th, 1993, I had a mandate to deal with the difficult places in the world, and thus it was that I as a staffer for the committee made four trips to the former Yugoslavia between 1991 -- in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's come back to that in a few moments. Let me proceed just a bit through your professional experiences, and then obviously we'll come back more specifically to your professional involvements in relation to the former Yugoslavia. After leaving the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, you were then appointed ambassador -- in fact, the first United States ambassador to the Independent Republic of Croatia, and you served in that capacity from approximately the 24th of June, 1993, until the 3rd of January, 1998?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Following that, sir, is it correct that from approximately 1998 to 2003 you taught at the United States National War College?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct, but with a -- about a 20-month [Realtime transcript read in error "20-minute"] period in which I was seconded to the United Nations Transitional Administration in East Timor in 2000 and 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your involvement was in East Timor and any positions you held there?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: If I can note for the transcript I said a 20-month, not a 20-minute period. The -- I was the director for political, constitutional, and electoral affairs for the United Nations which made we responsible for, among other things, the political transition in east Timor, and then in July 2000 an interim government was formed in east Timor, with an eight-member cabinet, and so I was one of the cabinet members with responsibility -- the formal title was first cabinet minister for political affairs, which included the foreign affairs function. Later an East Timorese was headed -- came on to be head of foreign affairs and I -- my title became cabinet member for political affairs in Timor Sea -- which political affairs was the constitutional transition;, Timor Sea was negotiations with Australia over oil and gas resources in the Timor Sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And after this approximately 20-month period, then you returned to teach again at the national war college for a time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I understand, sir, that you have recently published a book called -- titled "The End of Iraq."

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That's right, The End of Iraq: How American Incompetence Created a War Without End.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies, we're speaking a bit too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ambassador, if we can then go specifically to your time as ambassador to the Republic of Croatia. Again, you served in that capacity for approximately late June of 1993 and continued until the 3rd of January, 1998. And I take it in that capacity you did -- not to make it sound normal, but the types of duties that an ambassador in an embassy would have in other embassies around the world, albeit in the former Yugoslavia at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges briefly some of the major projects or aspects of what was happening at former Yugoslavia -- in the former Yugoslavia at that time that you were most directly involved in?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived, of course I was the first US ambassador to Croatia, although there was already an embassy there. But naturally, I did the kinds of activities that one would undertake -- newly arriving in a country and establishing diplomatic relations at the ambassadorial level, meeting government officials, explaining US policy, travelling around the country. But the major focus for the first ten months of my tenure was on the Muslim-Croat war that was underway in Bosnia, and the -- a US effort to try to stop the atrocities that were taking place and then -- and then the successful effort to bring that war to a conclusion with the Washington Agreement, and I participated in the negotiations that led to the Washington Agreement. From -- in 1994 and 1995, in addition to all the issues that were related to the implementation of the Washington Agreement and other issues related to Bosnia, I also was very heavily involved in the Croatia peace process as -- first, as one of the co-sponsors of negotiations that led to a cease-fire between the Republic of Croatia and the Krajina Serbs. Then as one of the authors of the so-called Z-4 peace process which was an effort to find a peaceful solution to the Krajina problem with substantial autonomy for the Serb-majority areas in Croatia, that failed with -- when the issue was settled militarily in Operation Storm and then finally I was the co-mediator of the Erdut peace agreement which was concluded on the 12th of November, 1995, that ended the war in Croatia by providing for the peaceful reintegration of Serb-held eastern Slavonia into Croatia. And then after that I served as the de facto chairman of the Article 11 commission of that agreement, which monitored the implementation of that agreement and the other activity -- major activities were those that -- and participated in the Dayton Peace Treaty negotiations. And then naturally a major focus was to help ensure Croatian compliance with the conditions of the Dayton Peace Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Stepping back for one moment you mentioned a few moments ago that before becoming ambassador you had travelled on official business or mission, if you will, in the former Yugoslavia, on at least four prior [microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During your time on Senate Foreign Relations, did you write a report titled "ethnic cleansing in Bosnia and Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And approximately when was that and generally what was that report about, other than what's disclosed in the title of course?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was in August of 1992. It was a response to -- a mission that was undertaken in response to disclosures in the American and international press about Serb-run concentration camps. And so we went out to document that. And in the course of doing that and of interviewing refugees who had come out of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we -- we -- I can't -- we discovered or reported on the camps but also a much larger pattern of the ethnic cleansing, the systematic expulsion of Bosnian Muslims and Croats by the Serbs from large areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So in fact, ambassador, you had some extensive -- fairly extensive dealings and background in the former Yugoslavia and the issues that were developing -- had or were developing there prior to taking on your position as ambassador. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I certainly had some background, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going to your time after arriving -- taking up your post in Zagreb, can we begin on this topic by -- let me ask you, who are your principal contacts in the Croatian government during this -- for now let's concentrate on the 1993/1994 time period.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Of course I had many contacts in the -- among the -- virtually all the ministers in the Croatian government, military commanders, parliamentarians, local officials. But the most important of these, of course, was President Franjo Tudjman, whom I saw on a regular basis, and the foreign minister, Mate Granic, and the defence minister, Gojko Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In these earlier years, these years from 1993 to the end of 1994, did you meet with President Tudjman, would you say frequently?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes -- I would say quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Several times a week?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That would be -- that would be quite usual, and as things went into crisis mode, as they often did, it could be several times a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before going forward with your dealings with those individuals and others, let me just mention one other individual. During your time as ambassador, did you ever meet an individual named Slobodan Praljak?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: So far as I recall, I met him once at Zagreb airport very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going back to President Tudjman, Susak and Granic, as you became with these men, can you tell the Judges what you observed and learned about President Tudjman's territorial aspirations, if any, concerning Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: President Tudjman believed that Bosnia and Herzegovina would not and should not continue as a sovereign, independent state, and that a substantial part of Bosnian territory should become territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did he ever explain to you the basis for these views or ...

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, he had -- he had many theories. First, that the Bosnian -- Bosniaks or Bosnian Muslims were not a real nation, that they were Croats who spoke the Croatian language, who had converted to Islam, and therefore they didn't have an authentic claim to a state. That of course was the state of these -- of three nations that didn't want to be together, that historically the territory of -- part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina had belonged to Croatia. He referred specifically and very often to the 1939 agreement that established the Banovina of Croatia, that included parts of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He also referred to the map of the NDH Croatia, fascist Croatia during the Second World War which also included a large part of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did President Tudjman ever show you maps or during your -- or -- and/or during meetings with him did you ever see maps of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which indicated how it might be divided?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. He had a number of maps to show what might become part of Croatia or how it might be divided between the -- a Croatian -- and sometimes -- well, to show how it might be divided, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges what you recall about the configuration of borders that he proposed which might have been different over time or different models, but can you tell the Judges about that.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: To be clear, he would -- he wouldn't show maps that would show this territory as being formally annexed into Croatia, but the context made it clear that this is what he thought should become part of Croatia. But the -- the maps would certainly include the Herzegovina, Posavina, often they followed very similar to the map of the Banovina of Croatia. But also he had ideas about population transfers and that one map showed Bosnia being divided right down the middle with -- therefore, Banja Luka becoming part of the Croatian side and Tuzla part of the Serbian side. He would talk approvingly of the idea population transfers. He often made the point about Banja Luka, that although it was a Serbian city, it really looked more to Zagreb than it did to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Staying on maps and territory, did the topic of Mostar ever come up in your conversations with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did he say about that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That it was a Croatian city in one -- well, that it was the capital of -- of the Croatian republic, if there was going to be a three-republic solution. That the Muslims had no real claim to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges a bit more when you were involved in -- with conversations or dealings with President Tudjman in connection with various peace discussions, whether that was various cease-fires or the Washington Agreement or Dayton, how these factors or how these views of his in terms of territory would impact his thoughts and his efforts -- his involvement with peace efforts.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: President Tudjman was one of the easiest people in the world to read. No matter how much he tried to -- might try to -- no matter how much it might be good for Croatia for him to restrain his true agenda, it almost always came through. So he would present these -- even when it was clear that we were about to conclude an agreement on one set of terms and with one map, it wouldn't stop him from -- even at the last minute when there was absolutely no hope that anybody would accept any different version and certainly not his version, which we all recognised as a -- as reflecting his desire for Greater Croatia, he nonetheless would come forward and say: Well, what about this map? And frankly that happened at all stages in this process. It happened just after the Washington Agreement was concluded. It happened after the Dayton Agreement was concluded in the period between the conclusion of Dayton on the 21st of November and its formal signing in the Elysez palace in December, obviously a time when anybody else would have understood that the map was not going to be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We focussed -- I focussed my questions to you and you focussed your answers so far primarily on President Tudjman. Can you tell the Judges whether in your experience Defence Minister Susak held similar views?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Similar but not identical. The first point about Susak is that he was a loyal lieutenant of President Tudjman, which perhaps is one reason why he was so effective. He would refer to him as the boss and if the boss made a decision, he was going to carry that out. On the other hand, he was going to go to the boss and to the president and bring a contrary point of view. But my impression of him and I spent a lot of him with him, is that Tudjman was an advocate, if you will, of a great Greater Croatia, a Greater Croatia that included a lot of -- perhaps a -- certainly a lot of Muslim-majority territory, perhaps a lot of Bosnian Muslims, whereas Susak I would describe as being in favour of a little Greater Croatia, that really the area that he wanted to incorporate into Croatia was Herzegovina, which of course was the part of Croatia where he was from.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador, I've been reminded that both of us, since we are both native English speakers and tend to speak quickly one after the other, to please give a bit of a pause for translation between our questions and answers, and that's directed at me as much as it is to you. In this regard, sir, in terms of these territorial issues, can you explain to the Judges in this context what was the US diplomatic or foreign policy strategy, if you will, in dealing with Tudjman and the Tudjman government on these issues as it related to accomplishing peace in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: The United States believed that the borders of the internationally recognised successor states of the former Yugoslavia could not and should not be changed, that the -- that the only way to have peace was for everybody to accept the borders of the states as they emerged in 1991, that is the borders that were the borders of the republics in Yugoslavia. That once you try to change any border, you were opening -- you were creating -- opening a can of worms, that is to say creating a situation that was likely to involve ever more demands for changes of borders and produce more conflict. And this had a very direct application to Croatia. From literally the day I presented my credentials until the conclusion of the peace process and perhaps I should say until the day I left Croatia, the -- our -- the US government message was very simple: We will -- we support the territorial integrity of Croatia to the extent that Croatia supports the territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And that if Croatia adopted a political approach that represented the territorial integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the United States would use its diplomatic and other influence to bring about a political solution to the problem in Croatia so that -- so that the occupied territories of Croatia, that is the Serb-held territories, would be re-integrated into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there any sense in which the US position was to put Tudjman to a choice, what he could have or what he could not have?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. The basic strategy was that Tudjman would have to choose between a Croatia within its 1991 borders that included the Krajina region and eastern Slavonia, Baranja, the city of Vukovar, that would be -- and -- and also beyond the path to integration into western institutions, to include eventually NATO and the European Union, that would be one choice. The other would be to pursue the dream of a Greater Croatia by taking territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina with no prospect that he would be successful at that and no chance that the United States would ever grant international recognition to that effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was going to put some questions to you about Tudjman's views toward the Muslims and toward Bosnia, but in fact you've touched on most of those -- or answered those questions primarily already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I'd like to ask a follow-up question because the ambassador has just been speaking about a very important problem. You've just said that when you presented your credentials to President Tudjman, you set out your country's position in order to -- and you said that there could be no modification of frontiers, of borders, as they were in 1991. Is that what you said, that the 1991 borders should be preserved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was our -- that was our -- our position. There was in the -- I suppose I should have a small addendum here. There was some discussion in this period of possible corridors to the sea that might have involved some territorial changes. But the basic point was, first, that there would be absolutely no changes brought about by force and without the consent of all the parties; and second, that as a practical matter, you could not have changes in borders because once you started down that path it would never end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And your country's position was shared, I assume, by the international community, that is to say the other countries, the other states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, that is correct. Certainly the entire international community insisted that there could be no changes in borders brought about by force; and if there were any changes, they could only occur through the consent of all the parties. David Owen, the -- the -- one of the co-chairman of ICFY and who had responsibilities for peace negotiations came up with a number of schemes that did involve territorial changes of these international borders. And these schemes, frankly, always made us very uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador, for purposes of the record, could I get you to explain further when you say references to ICFY, what that was?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was the international conference for the former Yugoslavia, a committee of European states and the United States. It was co-chaired by a representative of the United Nations and by a representative of the European Union. Cyrus Vance was the initial UN representative, later Thorvald Stoltenberg and then the EU representative was Lord David Owen or co-chairman I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question. Your government's position was quite clear and despite that, President Tudjman each time seemed to broach that question of a Greater Croatia again during your negotiations or discussions and showed you maps, et cetera. So he didn't seem to understand the position taken by the international country -- by the international community and your own country vis-a-vis Croatia or did he try to convince you and to convert you to his way of thinking, along with the other countries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was totally convinced of the logic, the historical justice, and the correctness of his position. And so he was certain that he -- if he kept explaining it to others, me, the members of congress, members of the Clinton administration, that we would eventually understand the logic and this is why he kept at it no matter how strongly we insisted that we were not going to agree to changes in borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps just one additional question on terms of President Tudjman's views toward Bosnia as a state. Did he ever describe its existence and its borders as "unnatural"?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in what sense?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, in the sense that Bosnia and Herzegovina had never existed as an independent state, in the sense that the Muslims were not a nation, that the Muslim nationality was a communist construct of the Tito Era, that -- I think he believed that states ought to be ethnically homogenous or close to it. He often spoke approvingly of the 1923 transfer of population between Greece and Turkey, which I must say I found, you know, rather odd as I often reminded him it wasn't as if things subsequently worked out very well between Greece and Turkey in the intervening 70 years, but he kept coming back to that. He considered -- I think that -- basically, he was very much prejudiced against the Muslims as a people. He also saw that -- he believed that there -- that the Balkans was the fulcrum of three civilisations, western civilisation of which Croatia was then the eastern frontier, the Orthodox civilisation stretching from Serbia through Russia, and then an Islamic tip of the sword or spear as represented by Bosnia and the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the issue of population transfer or exchanges, during your tenure as ambassador and in dealing with these issues did you ever hear or come across a phenomenon which some might call either reverse ethnic cleansing or self cleansing?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: There were I think two places where we saw that. First, in Bosnia where the -- where the Croatians had a basic strategic problem. The census of 1991 showed that the Croat population of Bosnia was 17 per cent, which of course made it by far the smallest of the three communities. And they were located, among other places, in western Herzegovina which was more or less purely Croat or -- Central Bosnia and in the Posavina region. But in reality - and this -- Croatian officials including Susak would often talk to me about - the Croatian population was smaller than 17 per cent, maybe as small as 10 or 12 per cent. Why? Partly the result of Croatian policies. Tudjman -- Croatia had a policy of granting Croatian citizenship to any ethnic Croat who wanted it, and of course as compared to Bosnia and Herzegovina in this period, Croatia was both -- much more prosperous and much more peaceful. So not surprisingly, a lot of Croats voted with their feet and moved to Croatia, reducing the Croat population in Bosnia, and therefore weakening Croatia's claim to territory that it wanted to hold. So there was an idea that you might actually move the Croat population out of Central Bosnia or places in Central Bosnia where they were a minority or surrounded by the Bosnian Muslims and relocate them to Herzegovina, thus building up that population. The other example of reverse ethnic cleansing was by the Serbs where Milosevic encouraged the Serbs in the Krajina region to relocate to Kosovo in order to build up the Serbian population there, and that was not a very successful venture.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before moving forward, I'd like to ask you about some other senior Croatian officials at the time. When you were having these conversations and dealings with people like Tudjman, Susak, and others, did you ever have any contact or meetings with senior Croatian officials which had different views or opposing views to those of Tudjman and Susak?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: First and probably most influential was Mate Granic, the foreign minister who was and is an extremely decent human being. Before becoming foreign minister, he had been responsible for refugees and humanitarian affairs. Croatia had a terrifically good record of taking refugees. I can't think of a country that may -- has taken -- took so many refugees per capita and treated them reasonably well. Granic helped set that policy. During the period of 19 -- the first six months of my tenure when I was constantly raising the issue of HVO-run camps and the bad conditions in them, the problem of humanitarian convoys, the problem of the shelling of east Mostar, Granic was sympathetic. He sent foreign ministry officials into Bosnia. He attempted to deal with the problem, so he was very positive. Two other officials I would mention, Josip Manolic and Stipe Mesic, who broke with Tudjman around this period because of their opposition to Tudjman's policies in Bosnia. They felt that -- that Tudjman's policies were doing great damage to Croatia, that it was going to lead to sanctions on Croatia, to international pariah status, and they were right, it was heading in that direction. So they very much supported the idea of a unitary -- a unified Bosnia and Herzegovina, that Croatia should fully respect Bosnia and Herzegovina's international boundaries, it should stop its support for the HVO and for the Bosnian Croats, and bring an end to the Muslim-Croat war. And frankly, one of the things that helped enormously in our efforts to end the Muslim-Croat war was the fact that there was not a lot of support among the Croatian public for either a great Greater Croatia or a little Greater Croatia. There was on a popular level a lot of sympathy for the Bosnian Bosniaks or the Bosnian Muslims, a lot of sympathy for the people in east Mostar and in Sarajevo. And I remember, as an example of this, most vividly attending the liberal party conference, their annual conference and hearing the head of the liberal party, Drazen Budisa say basically that if Croatia continued -- if the Tudjman government continued its policies in Bosnia, Croatia deserved international sanctions. Of course he was a politician, he was saying it because there was a large segment of the Croatian people who did not want these kinds of policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, for the transcript at line 18, page 21, you said about the six first months where you met Mr. Mate Granic and in the transcript it says 19 but not the exact year. So what year was it actually?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we move on, going back to Mr. Mesic and Manolic, did they come back to you about intervening with Tudjman in any particular way or what position they hoped you would take?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke to them on a number of occasions in late summer/early autumn of 1993. They were extremely concerned about what Tudjman was doing in Bosnia, and they said there's nothing -- basically they said: There's very little we can do. You're the only person that he will listen to you. You've got to do -- you know, bring -- do everything you can. Bring all the pressure you can bring to bear to get Tudjman to -- to stop his support of the HVO and to stop the Muslim-Croat war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With all of this by way of -- well, more than an introduction, we're very substantively into your evidence now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask that the witness be shown P09498.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can I follow-up on the last issue. Would you tell the Bench something about Tudjman's reactions. First, did you try to follow suit, did you try to influence Tudjman, and what was his reaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly tried to influence Tudjman. This was the -- it was the substance of most of my interactions with Tudjman and I delivered on behalf of my government very strong warnings about the consequences of Croatia continuing these policies. Tudjman's reaction -- Tudjman's reactions were several. First, to -- sometimes he would argue that, yes, these terrible things are taking place, but the otherwise is doing it as well, the Muslims are doing the same things. And I would tell him: That is no excuse for your behaviour. We are going to hold Croatia accountable for what Croatia does and since Croatia supports the HVO, we hold Croatia accountable for what the HVO does. And it is totally irrelevant as to what the Bosnian Muslims are doing. So that was one set of exchanges where he would respond by saying: Yes, but the other side is doing the same thing. The second response was that as he -- as he -- it began to filter through to him just how serious we were and how perilous Croatia's position was, he would then promise to take action to correct the abuses that I was citing. And in fact, because he exercised very substantial control over the HVO, the Croatian government did correct these abuses. And eventually, we were able to bring the Muslim-Croat war to an end in February of 1994. He -- I do not recall him denying in any way the facts that I was presenting to him. So the reactions were either to say the other side was doing it or to -- to basically say: Yes, I'll try to do something about this -- well, also -- he would say you know, I -- it's a terrible situation down there, they're out of control, often referred to the HVO leadership as being out of control. But then he would say: Yes, I'll do something about it, and then in fact he would do something about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just said that you've informed Tudjman about a number of facts, of events, and that he told you that the Muslims were doing exactly the same thing. Could you please be more specific about this. What events, what facts, did you report to him exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this time I focussed on the following events. First, the blockage by the HVO of humanitarian convoys, convoys carrying humanitarian supplies to the government-controlled parts of Bosnia and also to east Mostar. Second, the holding of Bosnian Muslims in inhumane conditions in detention camps, and we pushed both to improve the conditions in the detention camps and for the unconditional release of the prisoners. Third issue was the shelling of east Mostar, a civilian area which, you know, there were large numbers of civilian casualties as well as the destruction of a culturally important area. And more generally, our insistence that the Muslim-Croat war be ended and that there be a peace agreement between these two communities. These were the matters that I was bringing to his attention on a very regular basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may insist, you have told us that when you put such complaints, as it were, to President Tudjman he never denied the facts, he admitted that there were doubtful, unlawful detentions under inhumane conditions and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. He never said: Oh -- he never said: Oh, the camps are fine. What are you talking about? He readily acknowledged that the -- or he never challenged that -- my assertions about the conditions in the camps, some of which were based on first-hand reporting by embassy officers. He simply said -- well, I mean, he would say: I'm not responsible, or the HVO leadership is not -- they're not fully under my control, but I will try to do something about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We were about to go I think to Exhibit P09498.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me make the situation concerning many of these documents very clear. The position of the provider, of the United States government, is that they can be discussed and shown and used in the court-room, but for purposes of, if you will, the record and keeping them in the future and access to the hard-copy documents themselves, they would be maintained by the registry under seal. However, we need not go into private session now to deal with the documents orally or to present them electronically. So with that in mind, if we could go, please, to exhibit P09498.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I'm trying to understand what you've just said. You said that the government of the United States of America would like these documents to remain under seal. These documents, in other words, will not be disclosed outside of this court-room, but at the same time you are telling me that these documents can be put to the witness because from what I understand they are not being fed into the e-court system. But if we put the document to the witness, then the document will become a public document because we'll ask the witness, for example, to read the third paragraph of this telegram and then the document becomes public. So I'd like things to be extremely clear with regards to this document. I'd like have to a clear idea about the position of the United States with -- as far as these documents are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me say it again, Your Honour. The concern is that the hard-copy document itself not be freely available to members of the public. If a member of the public were to talk into the registry and say: I would like to have a copy of that document and carry a physical hard copy of that document out of the building, that would not be allowed. The documents would be maintained by the registry under seal and they would not be publicly available. That's the principal concern that the government -- the United States government doesn't want the hard copy of the documents floating about the world and potentially manipulated in some fashion. However, the documents can be discussed in the court-room for the purposes of this case and can be broadcast, but no one will be able to get a copy of the document and take it somewhere. The difference between the hard copy -- maintaining the hard copy under seal, versus the information that the witness will discuss in the court-room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So you are telling me that the document can be displayed with the e-court system and it can also be seen and read from the outside of this court-room. Since our trial is broadcast, if the document is displayed on a screen, let's imagine someone living in a given country, country X, this person can then reproduce the document or copy the document and then let's imagine that the document is published in a newspaper, newspaper Y. Then we'll have a violation of the protective measures you're asking for. So how can we prevent such a thing? Because if the document is displayed on the screens --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure how it would be done electronically, Your Honour, unless someone had some sort of a screen-capture capacity. I believe I've accurately stated the position, and I will double-check with the representatives of the United States government, if you'll give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have accurately stated the United States position, Your Honour. It is not the broadcast of the information, it is the sealing of the hard-copy document in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then we'll proceed that way, but I think I've stated that with the modern technology anybody outside of this court-room can reproduce the document. But proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can then look, please, at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have it in front of you, Ambassador, can you tell the Judges what this document is.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it is a cable that I sent reporting on my presentation of credentials to President Tudjman and the conversation that we had subsequent to the presentation of credentials ceremony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this was on the 28th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges -- when a new ambassador normally presents his credentials to the head of state or the appropriate senior official of the host government, if you will, is that typically a bit of a formal procedure one would not expect to get into perhaps a lengthy, substantive discussion of policy?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Generally that's true. It is a formal ceremony with perhaps -- in which the ambassador hands over his letter of credentials, makes a brief statement on the desire for good relations with the country to which he has now presented credentials. There is a response, and perhaps a brief conversation that deals mostly with pleasantries.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what happened on your first meeting with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: We sat down and had an hour-long conversation on a variety of substantive issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking at the beginning, the summary and comment part of the document, you report -- is this a cable that you drafted?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Or under your supervision?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Actually both. But a cable from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it says: "In an unexpectedly lengthy conversation following by presentation of credentials this morning (June 28), President Tudjman sought US support against what he described as an Owen proposal that Croatia cede its own territory to facilitate a deal on Bosnia." Now, there are various peace aspects of that. In the interests of time, because as the President's explained our time is a bit limited, can I then direct your attention, please, with the usher's assistance to the second page. Halfway down the page there is a heading and it says: "And a Muslim route to the sea?" And then the cable goes on to say: "The second unacceptable proposal that Owen was trying to force on Croatia, according to Tudjman, was Muslim access to the Adriatic by ceding to them Croat-inhabited areas of B-H and another part of Croatia proper." And then skipping a few lines and then I'll ask you to comment on this. Skipping a few lines down it goes on to say that: "Tudjman added that Owen was also proposing to give the Muslims the east bank of the Neretva in Mostar and southward. Tudjman said that he failed to see why Owen was now insisting in territorial shifts unacceptable to the Croatian people and clearly against their strategic interest." Now, first of all, is that as you recall an accurate summary of your conversation with President Tudjman at the time and what more can you comment on his position?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is an accurate summary of the conversation that I had with him, and I think the cable speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I asked you some minutes ago now about how Tudjman's territorial views would enter into his views or actions taken in connection with various peace agreements or peace efforts. Can you tell the Judges, is this an example of that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is. There -- there are several points, I think, that are interesting here. First he discusses -- he says he's opposed to any territorial swap except possibly, if I could just look at the first -- at the summary again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, except possibly involving a part of the Vojvodina and this is because for reasons that frankly I never understood and I don't think were shared by hardly anybody else in Croatia, he was almost always willing to consider giving up the Baranja region of Croatia because it had not been part of the 1939 sphere or zone. This is the north-east corner of Croatia, north of the -- of -- of Vukovar and what's -- and eastern Slavonia. He -- he certainly did not want to give the Serbs a corridor north of the Sava, as was being asked by Owen. And as I said before, that kind of territorial concession was that -- that Owen was pursuing, my view very much on his own initiative, was not one that we were very sympathetic to. The final point here of course is that he was also treating territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina as if it were part of Croatia or at least it was part of his responsibility in opposing giving -- having that territory become part of a Muslim republic or Muslim entity within a federal Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm also struck by this aspect, and I wonder whether you are also thinking of the first of the two sentences on page 2 that have been read out. "Tudjman complains that he was asked to cede Croat-inhabited areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina." That's how I read this, as meaning he talks as if it was his Croatia already and complains that he is asked not to keep it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Precisely. He's not actually treating it any differently than the territory of Croatia itself, and you have it exactly right, that he is the leader, the president, of -- not only the Republic of Croatia but the ultimate president of the -- responsible for the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and therefore he is being asked to cede territory that belongs to the Croat nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very briefly, following up, Your Honour, it appears that Mr. Owen is coming to Tudjman, that's how I read it, that it's Owen's proposal, not Tudjman's proposal. So it's Owen that's looking to Tudjman as if Tudjman believes that the Croats over there need protection or what have you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, Mr. Praljak is on his feet. Why, Mr. Praljak, why are you on your feet? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Well, I want to put right a mistake, Your Honour. It was said, Mr. Galbraith said -- spoke about the corridor north of Sava. Now, north of Sava is Croatia, so I don't know what corridor he had in mind there and I think we ought to clarify that point because we all spoke of the corridor south of the Sava, which would link Serb territories with Krajina, and I think that would be the correct way of putting it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So apparently there is a problem in relation to geography. So what corridor are we talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me be clear. The Defence counsel is correct that this was a proposal from David Owen that Croatia concede to the Bosnian Serbs territory of the Republic of Croatia itself that is north of the Sava River so that there could be a corridor that would link western -- sorry, eastern part of Bosnian Serb territory with the western part of the Bosnian Serb territory, including of course Banja Luka. That was David Owen's proposal, and it did involve a change in the international borders. And Tudjman was asking for American support in opposing David Owen's proposal. He also asked for American support in opposing another David Owen proposal that would have had the Republic of Croatia, that is the -- within the 1991 borders, concede some territory that would enable the -- a Bosnian republic in the union of three republics to have -- and the Bosnian Serbs for that matter to have direct access to the sea. In the same conversation, he also made the point -- he also talked about David Owen asking him to cede territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina that was east of the Neretva, talking about it as if it was indistinguishable from the territory of the republic -- that he, Tudjman, was considering it indistinguishable from the territory of the Republic of Croatia. Now, to be clear, Owen would have been asking him to be consider territorial concessions about Croatia within its 1991 borders. He would not have been asking Tudjman -- would not have been asking Tudjman as the responsible party to actually make the concessions in Bosnia, but rather to use his influence with the Bosnian Croats to make those concessions But what's important about this cable is that Tudjman looks at it, because I'm after all reporting Tudjman's position, Tudjman looks at it as if it was indistinguishable from the territory of Croatia itself. And just to repeat, we, the United States, did not want to see territorial concessions -- changes in borders. We were not very supportive of this approach of David Owen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On that very point, if I can ask that we please go to the fourth page of the document under the heading "US-Croatian ties." Second paragraph. "I told Tudjman that the US supports Croatia's territorial integrity and that the basis of a close by lateral relationship lay in shared commitment to democracy, respect for human rights, and respect for the territorial integrity of other sovereign states. I pointed out that the discussion in the United States about sanctions on Croatia focussed on Croatian activity in Bosnia contrary to these principles." Sir, is that consistent with the strategy and position of the United States that you've now mentioned several times this morning?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is a very precise articulation of US policy which remained absolutely constant throughout my tenure as US Ambassador to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finishing with this document, if we can go to the last page and the last paragraph. Is it correct, sir, that at the end of the meeting in fact the word here "reiterated." You stated to Tudjman that the United States did not favour alteration under duress of one party of recognised international Bosnian parties."

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That was the strongly held position of the United States. It was a constant message -- a message that I was constantly delivering to Tudjman in the -- in the strongest possible terms in the course of my tenure as ambassador to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the time, and this may be a time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We'll have a 20-minute break and we'll resume around ten to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's ten to 11.00. Mr. Scott, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to go next to P09499 [Realtime transcript read in error "P04099"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a mistake with the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 9499, a cable from the 6th of July, 1993. Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, going on to this, is this a cable, a further cable, sent from Zagreb while you were ambassador concerning your dealings with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to direct your particular attention to paragraph 4, as a starting point. "Tudjman also downplayed his influence with the Bosnian Croats 'I have some political influence, but on the ground it is a situation that cannot be controlled.' He said that depending on the situation in a given region, the Croats and Serbs either 'collaborate or fight each other.'" In terms of President Tudjman's influence over the Croats, we will deal with that extensively in the course of your testimony. Let me ask you for now to direct your attention to the second part of that paragraph, collaboration with the Serbs. What was your knowledge at the time, information about the collaboration or cooperation between the Croats and Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: There was military cooperation between the HVO and the Bosnian Serb army, specifically it included circumstances in which the Serbs might allow the HVO to pass through Croatian line -- sorry, the Serbs would allow the HVO to pass through Serbian lines for the purpose of attacking the Bosnian government, the army. It included the Serbs providing tanks or artillery support for an HVO attack, and perhaps some that went the other way as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the phrase during this time or was it said there was something called "rent a tank?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, the notion that for" a certain number of marks, at this point I don't remember the price, you could rent a tank for a day and then you would pay so much for each shell that was fired, and of course these would be Serbian tanks that would be rented by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going on to the second page and item number 5, paragraph number 5. Again, on some of these matters, sir, I'm afraid we're going to have to move rather quickly to finish your testimony in the allotted time, but if you look in paragraph 5, are the notes that you have made here consistent with what you have told us earlier this morning about Tudjman's views about Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I think this illustrates his prejudice about the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For example halfway through the paragraph it says: "He pointed out that Croats and Muslims share a language, but 'the Islamic religion separates them.'"

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, and that reflected his view that the Muslims were Croats who had chosen Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to paragraph 6, and I will ask -- probably spend a bit more on this paragraph. It says: "Tudjman acknowledged the problems which the situation in BH or it say may BiH creates for Croatia and said 'I don't know how it happened.' But, he said, Croats are not conquering 'other'' territory, but 'land which for centuries has belonged to Croats.'" Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It reflected his view that a -- a significant part of Bosnia was historically Croat territory and even if there were places that were no longer Croat inhabited, they were historically Croat and therefore could not be ceded to the Bosnian Muslims or the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going to paragraph number 8, starting with the first part of it before continuing. "Tudjman, not denying that Croatian support for the HVO is a reality." Had you raised with him, even by this time, the relationship and support between the Republic of Croatia and Herceg-Bosna and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. Our position was that Croatia supports, sponsors, and directs the HVO and the Bosnian Croat political parties, including the -- or the -- it supports the HVO, it supports the so-called government at Herceg-Bosna. It -- the -- it is the same -- was the same political party, the HDZ. And therefore, we were holding Croatia responsible for the actions of the HVO and of the Bosnian Croat authorities. And in this paragraph, of course, Tudjman is not denying that that is true; he's simply explaining it, namely that the Herzegovinians were -- provided critical support to Croatia in its hour in need in 1991, he's explaining that Herzegovina is part of the ancient kingdom of Croatia, that Herzegovina is strategically important to Croatia, which is obvious if you look at a map. It's of course no justification for Croatian territorial ambitions there or Croatian control, but he's simply explaining why it's important. And of course comes back, as he often does, to that 1939 agreement for the Banovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that's in his item -- reference 4?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May I next ask the witness to be shown P03 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to another exhibit, I'd like to go back to paragraph 4 where you said that Mr. Tudjman told you that there was certain situations in which there was cooperation -- or rather collaboration between Serbs and Croats and he quoted two examples. For example, sometimes the HVO would cross Serb lines to attack the Muslims, and then the other issue of the location -- tanks. Now, what you said that Mr. Tudjman told you, was that corroborated by your own information? Did your own information bear that out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, what I described to you about the -- the HVO renting Serbian tanks, using -- using the Serb artillery to support its military action to having transit through Serbian lines to attack the government, these are not things that Tudjman told me. This is based on information that -- that we had from -- on our own. What Tudjman said in this conversation is simply what is reported here, which is that the Croats and the Serbs in a given situation, either collaborate or fight each other. He did not provide those details, but the Prosecutor had asked me a separate question about the cooperation, and that's what I was describing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but this collaboration between the Serbs and Croats on the basis of what you knew, was that decided at a political level, high-up political level, or was it decided on the ground and were they agreements between the various military offices that reached this agreement without the top-most political authorities being aware of that? What would you say? It's rather an extraordinary situation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I cannot -- I cannot answer that question definitively because I don't know at what level this cooperation was -- was authorised or took place. I can provide an informed speculation that certainly it took place on the ground among different commanders, and that the approval for that went some way up the chain of command. But at what level it was granted, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may just simply point out that in light of the questions that were posed by the Prosecutor and your last questions, now we are into the area of getting information or having knowledge from sources. As I've indicated, it's a known -- it's very well-known that the CIA was actively working out of the Croatian embassy and that the -- the American embassy, that is, and the American embassy was getting lots of information. We have representatives here from the state department. I certainly want to know all about where did this information come and I certainly would like to look at this information, not that I don't take the gentleman at his word, but there may be something in it that's exculpatory. And I raise this at this point in time because if we will not be allowed to have access to that information because of an objection by the American government, then I certainly would ask that we stay away from these sorts of questions because it would be -- it would violate our clients' rights of confrontation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ambassador, the sources you refer to, the Defence is putting forward a hypothesis, they're putting forward their case. You can answer or not answer, or you can say: They are the usual sources that an ambassador has recourse to. I don't know. Answer one of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all respect to the ambassador, my understanding is -- my instructions from the United States government is that under Rule 70 we would not be able to go behind as to sources of this particular type of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in that event, Your Honour, I would ask that the previous answers to the questions posed be -- I know we can't strike it from the record, but at least be noted that they're not to be considered because we are not allowed to cross-examine in these areas based on the fact that we do not have access to these sources. And I would also ask, Your Honour, for a cautionary instruction to the Prosecution not to solicit information which would cause the witness to say: Based on information that I received or based on knowledge I know, of which he's unable to tell us where that information came from. I understand the US policy, and I understand the predicament the gentleman is in, but we also have certain protections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have recorded what you've just said. Mr. Scott, please proceed within the frameworks of Article 70, of course -- Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If we could next go, please, to Exhibit P03240. It's a rather thick document. There's really only one reference in it. As soon as it's available. The record of a presidential meeting in Zagreb on the same day, the meeting between Ambassador Galbraith and Tudjman on the 6th of July, 1993. And if I could ask for the usher's assistance to take us to page 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can direct your attention to the middle of that page, the English-language version is being displayed on the left side. About the middle of the page the remark is attributed to President Tudjman. It appeared in New York in -- and then Susak intervenes and says: "In Toronto, too." And then Tudjman continues to speak: "At the Bosnian delegation. I had requested through our people ... and this confirms what is written there. Now the question is in what way we are going to present our policy because they still have not, and America today also (said) that we have to be careful and (Ambassador) Galbraith told me today that we have to be careful about our actions in Bosnia and Herzegovina, also because Croatia could come under sanctions for our assistance to the HVO. Hence, such a policy towards Croatia is continuing." And can you just tell us, sir, based on your meeting with Tudjman on that same day, has the president accurately reported the US position?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. In very brief, summary form -- but I would also underscore a point here, which is that he -- he admits, as he did in the conversation with me, or at least didn't deny, he admits that Croatia is providing assistance to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So when Mr. Tudjman -- when President Tudjman was speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Scott. Mr. Praljak was on his feet. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I think there was a misinterpretation. It says: "Towards Bosnia and Herzegovina" not "in Bosnia and Herzegovina." So policy towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, whereas in the translation it said "in Bosnia and Herzegovina." So it's the relationship, it's towards Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think the translation is -- I don't know -- I'm not sure what Mr. Praljak is referring to. What I quoted was: "Careful about our actions," that is Croatian government's actions, "in Bosnia and Herzegovina also because Croatia could come under sanctions for our assistance to the HVO. Hence, such a policy towards Croatia is continuing." THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May I read out the Croatian text? "Galbraith, we have to take into consideration our actions towards Bosnia and Herzegovina." "Prema" is the word used in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, counsel Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, Your Honour, what Mr. Praljak read out is the Croatian text of the records on page 40, according to the Prosecution's numbers, which corresponds to the English translation. So that must be the same number of pages. And it says "prema Bosnia and Herzegovina," which means towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, as Mr. Praljak said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the Croatian text we do indeed see the word "prema."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador, going back to the point you were making a moment ago, so we see here that when President Tudjman, Susak, and others are talking about this, if you will, among themselves, there is no denial that Croatia was assisting the HVO?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct. After all, he's saying Croatia could come under sanctions because of our assistance to the HVO, and that is entirely consistent with the position that he adopted in the meeting with me that I testified to in response to your earlier questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can next go on to Exhibit P05090.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, that on the 15th of September, 1993, you and the ambassadors from Germany and Turkey were called to a meeting with President Tudjman at the presidential offices?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you have a chance or if you've had a chance to look at this transcript, is that a record of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is a record of that meeting. I might add, though, that it is a record of a meeting mostly conducted in English that was translated into Croatian -- well, Tudjman would have spoken in Croatian, but the ambassadors all spoke in English, translated into Croatian, and re-translated back into English. So the speech is probably not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, by the way, when you would have these meetings with President Tudjman in his office, did you know you were being recorded?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking to the second page of the document, page number 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a technical precision. There was a transcriber who was next to you and recorded everything or did you have a technical device?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a microphone on the table or someplace else, if it was upstairs in his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So every time you knew that this would be recorded. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course you were never sure whether the microphones were running or not in any given meeting, and I never asked: Oh, is this being recorded? But I presumed that it was being recorded and I operated on the assumption that it was being recorded. But I suppose to be fully accurate, I didn't definitively know that it was being recorded until the Croatian government began to release transcripts, because at no point did any -- did any Croatian official tell me: Oh, it's being recorded. But there were recording devices, and so I presumed that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in this transcript or this record of the meeting on the 15th of September, 1993, President Tudjman says that he's describing to you certain discussions that he's had, recent discussions, with Izetbegovic. And again, if we can go to page 4 in the interest of time, looking to the paragraph or to the portion which says: "The second reason for calling you here is to inform you that we have signed this agreement which, remains secret, but we will inform your governments. It deals with the policy which should be conducted in BiH by both the Croatian and Muslim sides. This comes as a priority bringing together the Bosnian Republic of Croatia and the Bosnian Muslim Republic in order to enter into a confederation with the Republic of Croatia." Now, with that in mind, sir, can you tell us a bit about what this meeting was about, what was happening here as you understood it.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. The idea was that the essential point that came out of this was an agreement to form a federation of the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims, the Bosniaks, which in turn would enter into a confederation with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going on to page 5, Tudjman continues on that page, he says: "Mr. Izetbegovic also expressed one more thought. I think this agreement as it is, is in accordance with the interests of Croatia and, I believe, in line with the intentions of your government as well. This agreement stems from a unified existence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but bearing in mind that the Serbs practically separated from this union. In relation to that, the Croatian and Muslim republics should take a stance on this and position themselves for a confederation with Croatia. Mr. Izetbegovic is of the opinion that if the Serbs withdraw, or even without that, there may be the creation of an independent Bosnian Muslim Republic. He says that in that case such a Bosnian Muslim Republic would have international recognition of its borders. As acceptable as this may be to him, this would also mean that it would be acceptable for the Bosnian Croatian Republic to join in with Croatia." What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It certainly reflected Tudjman's wish for what he hoped would happen I think in a very stark way, namely that you would have a Bosnian Croat republic with established borders, you would have a separate Muslim republic, and then that Croat republic would join Croatia and become part of Greater Croatia. And it also reflected his logic in how he was going to get there, namely that the Serbs split-off and then you encouraged the Muslims to form their own state.
