I did not think, based on anything that I know, that this actually reflected the views of Izetbegovic, and so a great deal of what was going on in this meeting was he was trying to persuade the United States, Germany, obviously from Croatia's point of view the two most important countries of bilateral relationships, and Turkey, who he saw as being the most influential country with the Bosnian Muslims to accept this kind of solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going to page 7, as soon as we have it, your intervention, Peter Galbraith. "It seems to me there is some contradiction in the agreement as I see it. From one side the possibility of a union of the Muslim and Croatian Republics (BiH) has been discussed and on the other side its confederation with Croatia." Can you tell us more about what you saw as the contradiction and what Tudjman was saying.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. And I think, however, this sentence, it reflects the problem -- the lack of clarity that comes from speaking in English, translated into Croatian, and then back into English. So I will give you the idea, but perhaps the words here are not exactly the words that I said. And of course 13 years later I can't recall the exact words I would have said. But I certainly know what I thought, and I would have articulated what I thought, and that is there was an obvious contradiction between something we saw as very positive and, in fact, became the basis of the Washington Agreement, namely that you would have a -- a federation between the Bosnian Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats on the one hand, and on the other hand that perhaps the Croat -- there would be a Croat republic which would then join Croatia. The reason I think these words are imprecise is that -- is that we accepted the idea, and this was in the Washington Agreement and in fact in the Dayton Agreement as well, that the -- that the entities in Bosnia might have special relations with their neighbouring countries. Now, we never used the word "confederation," but we did go along with the concept of special relationships.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going -- finishing on this document, if we go to page 12, because I asked you earlier about the -- about the question of Mostar ever came up. And on the bottom of page 12, Ambassador Galbraith, you say: "What would happen if the Muslim republic becomes an independent country that includes Mostar?" And on the next page, page 13, Tudjman says: "Mostar is the capital of the Croatian republic (of BiH) that's not at stake here. "Galbraith: Do the Muslims accept that? "Tudjman: Yes, of course." And was that Tudjman's continuing view of the position and role of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And what he was -- you can see from this transcript that I'm asking a series of, if you will, leading or skeptical questions about this proposal to draw him out. But he -- what he basically is saying that: Oh, there's no problem -- they're saying: Not only does all of Mostar become part of the Croat republic, which it might eventually join Croatia, but that the Bosnian government, the Bosniaks, accept that. And as you might imagine I didn't actually believe that that was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can next then go, please, to Exhibit P06412.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification while we're doing -- while we're getting the next document. It's my understanding that this entire conversation is within the context of: If the Serbs break away and if the Muslims form their own republic, as opposed to: This is, you know, part of -- there's a plan A plus plan B. This is my understanding of the context. Am I right or --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why don't we wait until cross-examination for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The whole point is, as we go along why don't we make the record straight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Because I'm not going to use my time to ask your questions, Mr. Karnavas. I think the ambassador has been very clear that he himself knew very well what was happening here and he was drawing Tudjman out to state what his true views were. And the witness has said he was skeptical of what was really happening here. It was being presented as an Izetbegovic proposal, and the witness said he was skeptical of that. Now I'll ask the witness if I've properly understood his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is precisely right, and of course one of the reasons -- I was drawing this out for two reasons. First, so that my German and Turkish colleague would fully grasp what was going on here, and naturally we talked about it afterwards. And the fact that I'd drawn it out was some -- was information that then helped them see clearly through what Tudjman was talking about. So that was one very important point. And second, I was looking for information so that I could describe this clearly back to the United States government so that they would grasp what was going on here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could then go to P06412, transcript of a meeting on the 4th of November, 1993. And if we can just only go -- again in the interests of time, to page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: These are continuing discussions. You will see and if anyone in the court-room wants to skim through the transcript, continuing discussions of some of these concepts between you and President Tudjman. And if I can ask you to look at the bottom -- the last paragraph on page 7. Is it correct to say, sir, that you once again state the US position on borders to President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. And one of the things you have to understand is that the reason I'm constantly doing this is because it is clear to me that Tudjman is constantly -- it's -- it is the thing that is at the top of his mind that he wishes to change these borders. And I wished to close the door on that thought in every way I -- that is humanly possible. And hence, the statement here: "The most solid basis for a solution for an agreement between the individual parties lies in recognising the fact that the present borders are international borders and there is no prospect that they will ever be changed."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Ambassador, going now back to this concept, there was an earlier reference in one of the earlier cables to the question of Zagreb's or Tudjman's control over the HVO. And I said we would come back to that. Can you tell us what your observations and experience was on that topic, and that is to what extent did the Tudjman government control Herceg-Bosna and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: In my judgement and based on my experience, President Tudjman was de facto equally the president of the -- equally the president of the Bosnian Croat political entity, as he was the president of Croatia, that he was equally the commander-in-chief of the HVO as he was the commander-in-chief of the HV.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give the Judges some of the -- some of your basis for that, some of your experience, some of your conversations on which you base that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, let's take the -- sorry. Let's take the military command. Croatia financed the HVO, paid salaries. The Croatian -- Croatia appointed the generals and top officers of the HVO, and when it became convenient to change them it was Croatia that changed them. Croatian -- Croatian -- this was economically part of Croatia. It was the same political party which Tudjman headed in -- effectively in both countries, the HDZ. What later during the presidential campaign in Croatia, there were billboards in Bosnian Croat territory that referred to Tudjman as "our president." The -- and of course Bosnian Croats voted in the Croatia elections. When -- when we sought action, the address that we went to was primarily Croatia, and it was when we went to the -- to Zagreb, to Tudjman, to Susak, to Granic that we in fact got results and often very prompt results.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say that -- sorry, let me interrupt you there for clarification. When you say you sought action, when you sought action or results, where?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Sorry, when we sought action or results in Bosnia, in the Croat part of Bosnia, when we wished to have humanitarian convoys, we wished the HVO to stop blocking humanitarian convoys, when we wished to have prisoners released, when we wished to get access to prison camps in Bosnia, all of these things were things that we did through the government in Zagreb and direct -- usually by me directly with Tudjman, Susak, or Granic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On this topic, can you tell the Judges what your observations were about the level of knowledge or information displayed by Tudjman and Susak and others as to what was happening in the Croat parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the ground, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I think they knew what was going on in the Croat parts of Bosnia extremely well, better than what they in fact knew what was in fact going on in most parts of Croatia. And frankly, at this time they seemed to care more about what was going on in the Croat parts of Bosnia than they did about what was going on in the rest of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you share with the Judges any observations that you saw, experiences, in terms of whether Susak had any relationship, dealings, regular dealings, let me put it that way, with Boban. A. Oh, when I talked to Susak, he would often talk about his relations with Boban and their friendship and his -- his control or influence over Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In any of your conversations with Susak, do you recall any instance in which he claimed to have control or influence over any particular HV or HV commanders that were operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. He asserted that he had control over Slobodan Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Susak?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, Susak asserted that -- that he had effective control over Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I won't go into that further at this moment, Mr. Ambassador, and the Judges, because there will be a follow-up reflected in one of the upcoming documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I interject a question? We have been shown a lot of - I will carefully say - normative texts that organised the -- that Herceg-Bosna and the HZ HB. According to those texts, it would be the president of that entity that names, for instance, generals. Have you ever heard any reference to such documents. I now use the term unconstitutionality. Was there ever a discussion that all this teleguided action, as you describe it, from Zagreb was "anti-constitutional" in a Herceg-Bosna perspective?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So far as I recall, not at all. In short, the -- in short, Tudjman, Susak -- Tudjman and Susak, as best I can recall, never suggested that there was some constitutional impediment to their control over the Bosnian Croat political entity or over the HVO. Milosevic, by contrast, used this as a smoke screen all the time. Oh, well, that's a separate country. I don't control the Republika Srpska, I don't control the Bosnian Serb army, that's something different. That, as best I can recall, was never mentioned to me by Tudjman or Susak. They -- they didn't go through that charade. They took responsibility for the Bosnian Croat leadership and for the HVO. And I think it's important to understand the reason why this was. They were looking for good relations with the United States, and from the time of my arrival I think it's fair to say that they felt that they -- that relations with the United States were improving greatly, they felt, rightly, that I was sympathetic to Croatia, that the Clinton administration was sympathetic to Croatia, and that there was a partnership. So in the manner of what became an increasingly close partnership, they weren't going to pretend about structures that didn't matter to them; in other words, they were going to be direct with their partners, perhaps in a way they would not have been if they were dealing with less -- countries that they felt less close to. And of course at that time they had no idea that their actions were going to be being judged someday by a Tribunal like this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the views that you've expressed or the information or knowledge that you've indicated in the past few minutes, did you consider this was some knowledge uniquely known or held to you or what was the status of this information or knowledge in the international diplomatic community in Zagreb at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I think every diplomat who, except the most oblivious, clearly understood that Tudjman and Susak controlled Bosnian Croat political entity, the HDZ in Bosnia, and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say in that context, sir, that one might consider it was no secret at all or what some might call an open secret?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was an open secret, shading into no secret at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I can turn to Mr. Boban. Do you recall when you first had a meeting with Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when was that, please?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was in Split on July 20th, 1993, if I am right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how did that meeting come about and can you just give us a brief overview of what happened in that meeting, the nature of the conversation, the dynamics, what happened.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: The meeting took place in the Croatian naval base in Split. It was at the -- I think it was set up at the request of Boban. And it began I think around 5.00 in the evening and lasted two or three hours. It began with a long litany of complaints by Boban against the Bosnian government, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Bosniaks as a people. And then I think a great deal of surprise on his part when I responded very firmly about -- on the subject of HVO misconduct and atrocities, including the holding of prisoners in inhumane conditions, the blocking of humanitarian convoys, and the shelling of east Mostar. The -- he really was very much taken aback. I think he was -- he had believed from the statements that I had made about Croatia's territorial integrity, from a visit I'd make to Vukovar, from my denunciation of Vukovar as a war crime, that my sympathy and my government's sympathy for Croatia was unlimited. And in fact, the denunciation of war crimes committed by the Serbs was matched by denunciation war crimes committed by the HVO. He responded by promising to correct some of these problems. In particular he said that he would move to release prisoners. He didn't quite come out and say that, but that was the implication. The next day he sent a message to my office in Zagreb that in fact he was going to release prisoners and indeed prisoners were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's look, in fact, please, at the next Exhibit P09501. If we could enlarge the first paragraph, please, a bit. Thank you very much. If we can scroll down or scroll up, I guess, we can see the top part of the document in the English part. Thank you very much. Sir, is this a cable reporting your meeting with Boban on the 20th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And it also reports some of the actions that followed directly as a result of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You raise with him during this meeting such topics as UNHCR, the humanitarian convoys, and as you indicated a moment ago, the holding of a large number of Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you raise to him -- did you raise during this conversation or meeting that the state of Croatia possibly faced sanctions if the HVO did not, if you will, clean up its act?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, that was our position. We told Croatia that and I told him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. As you indicated a moment ago, you give a -- you give a report as to the beginning of the meeting, Boban's litany?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask, please, that we go to the second page. And the section that's titled "unimpeded access for humanitarian convoys."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was this an important issue to you and the US government at this time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Hugely important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what steps did you take to address it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I raised the issue with the responsible Croatian -- well, President Tudjman, with Defence Minister Susak, Foreign Minister Granic, other officials, and with Boban. I also -- the US government made clear that if humanitarian assistance did not go to the -- into the Bosniak areas in Bosnia, that it would result in sanctions -- in US support for sanctions on Croatia. It was a matter of the highest priority for my government that humanitarian supplies go into Bosnia and that the suffering that was caused by that war be mitigated to the greatest extent possible. And it was utterly unacceptable that Croatia and an entity -- for which Croatia was directly responsible as for which Croatia was funding should obstruct the flow of that humanitarian assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the second paragraph under this heading is it accurately reported, sir, that: "Ambassador Galbraith stated that denial of assistance to women and children is a war crime"?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I certainly stated that in the strongest possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going over to the next page, please, second paragraph -- the paragraph starting: "Galbraith said ..." I said we would probably come back to this -- this topic would come up again. In this meeting, according this to this cable, it says one of the things again was raised was in the middle of that paragraph that: "Croat-Serb military collaboration must cease." And was that the type of collaboration that you were describing earlier?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you also raise the issue and continue to raise the issue about the freedom of movement of international organisations such as the UN and UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That was an issue that we raised constantly. We wanted the UN to be able to carry out its mission and of course access for the ICRC was essential in order to -- for humanitarian reasons, in order to, you know, ensure that prisoners in camps were being treated properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you raise with Boban during this meeting the fact that by this time two Spanish officers had been killed in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was Boban's response to that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He blamed the Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The next heading is called -- is -- states: "Boban's agenda." And toward the end of that paragraph, that first paragraph, can you see that -- do you recall talking with Boban about the fact that they wanted to move -- there was a desire to move a large number of Croats from the Vares area?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did Mr. Boban give you any details, if you recall, I know this is years later, any details as to how it was that they would move this Croat population from the Vares area?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I don't recall if we discussed the mechanics of how they might be moved, but the point was that he wanted them moved from Vares to Croat-controlled areas, presumably Herzegovina, to increase the Croat population in Herzegovina. What was striking is that he did not ask for help in protecting the Croat population of Vares. He did not ask the United States to use its very considerable influence with the government in Sarajevo, for example, to do anything that might benefit the population in -- while they were still in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On item H, on the next page, there are a number of lettered items and there's letter H. And do you recall, sir, whether Boban then committed to you in this meeting that he would release 6.000 detainees "unilaterally, except for 'criminals'"?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we can go, because it immediately flows from this, to Exhibit P09500.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is this a cable that was sent on the 21st of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, was there a subsequent conversation around this time very close in time from Mr. Boban that in fact the release of prisoners had been started?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That day he contacted -- or his office contacted the -- my office in Zagreb to pass on a message that -- and I quote the message: "Today began a release of prisoners held by the HVO in a determined process that is continuing and will go on until all have been released."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can next ask you to look at Exhibit P09697. While that's coming up, Ambassador, you've indicated several times that one of the senior Croatian officials that you had frequent dealings with and apparently quite a bit of respect for was the foreign minister, Dr. Granic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'm now showing you the attachment or the second page of P09697, which is titled "an appeal." If you look at the bottom of the document around exactly the same time, the 21st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Does Dr. Granic's appeal relate, in fact, to the very issues that you and the United States government were raising with the Government of Croatia at this time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you will see on the cover -- the cover page, if you will, the first page of Exhibit P09697, that apparently the head of Mr. Granic's office, I assume his head of -- administrative aid or Chief of Staff was passing this or sending this appeal on to Jadranko Prlic, HZ HB HVO president. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me next ask you to please look at Exhibit P03673. And can you see, sir, if you can take a look at this, this is a -- it's titled: "Statement regarding the response by the President Dr. Prlic to the Republic of Croatia Deputy Prime Minister," who again is Dr. Granic, "Mostar, 23 July 1993." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if you look through the document, can you see that again it touches on such issues as humanitarian convoys and the detention and the holding of Muslim men? Take your time if you want to skim through it. It's a ...

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador, Mr. Ambassador, is this an example of -- of a situation you described to us some minutes ago where issues would be raised in Zagreb and you would -- you would see responses being made in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is an example, although I think it's -- would be correct to say that this method of communication from Granic to Prlic in the form of a demarche was probably -- and then a response was for the benefit of the United States because the way in which orders were transmitted was more direct. But this was a document that Granic produced to show he was doing something, which he genuinely was, and a response to the Granic demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we come back to some of the issues in more detail that you've indicated -- you've mentioned several times already today, the HVO detention camps, the humanitarian aid convoys, and the siege and the shelling of east Mostar. Is it correct, sir, that as of July of 1993 and thereafter you had raised all of these issues with Tudjman, Susak, Granic, and other officials that you were dealing with at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, how soon after taking up your post in Zagreb information came to your attention that the HVO was operating detention camps that were holding a large number of Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was very soon after taking up my post. I presented my credentials on the 28th of June, and I think we became aware of the round-up of men and, incidentally, some women - it's not true that it was just men - that took place a couple days later, I think on maybe the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During this phase of July, August, September 1993 approximately, were you responsible for sending two fact-finding missions into Bosnia-Herzegovina proper, Herzegovina specifically, and to certain islands on the Croatian coast?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And tell us about those two missions, why and what they found as an overview.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, one of my thoughts was that if we gained access to the prison camps, first the fact that they were being visited by the US embassy would certainly lead -- would hopefully lead - and I thought very likely lead - to improvements in the conditions in the camps. And I also knew that the Croatian government, while it might be prepared to block, delay, or obstruct visits by the ICRC and by the United Nations, would not dare to block a visit by the United States, so that we simply had more access than anybody else. So I wanted to get access to these camps. We sought access. Granic and Susak promised that we would get access, and indeed we did get access to the Heliodrom at Rodic, and I sent a team in there. It was also my very regular practice to send officers to interview refugees. This is actually something the US embassy had been doing from the start of the conflict in Bosnia. And indeed, I might add that a number of those testimonials have been submitted to this Tribunal. The -- but in any event, so we sent -- I sent people to Obonjan island and Gasinci refugee camp to interview people who had been in the Croatian detention camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you and the United States government continue to raise these issues with the Tudjman government and indicate that actions were expected -- corrections -- relief was expected or there could be consequences for Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour. [Interpretation] I apologise for having to interrupt but I'd like to clarify a point. In the transcript on page 63 when the witness mentioned Gasinci, line 12, I believe, and then in line 13 it says Croatian detention camps, that's the phrase used. I never heard the witness say that. Perhaps I didn't hear properly, but they were refugee camps. Could you have that checked, please, because I think I was listening to the English and I don't think the witness said detention camps, as it says here referring to Croatian detention camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think we can clarify that perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I had said was that I sent people to Obonjan island and Gasinci refugee camp to interview people who had been in the HVO-run detention camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The question I just put to you before the intervention was, did you and the United States government continue to raise these issues with the Tudjman government and again indicate that there might very well be sanctions or consequences for Croatia if the camp situation was not addressed?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: We constantly raised these issues, and I constantly made the point that we were -- that we would not judge Croatia on its commitments or what it promised to do, but on the results on the ground in the Croat part -- Croat-controlled part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As part of what was happening with the camps, did you come to know or have any information at the time that there was some programme or arrangement by which the Muslim men would be released from the camps, the HVO camps, if they would leave to a third country, leave Bosnia and go to a third country?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what can you -- do you recall -- looking at some of your documents in a few moments, but do you recall anything more about how that was done?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, this was reporting by some of the embassy officers who went to the refugee camps. And they described a process by which men held in these HVO camps were told that if they agreed to be re-settled in a third country, they would then be released from the camp, the HVO detention camp, and go to Croatia for a third-country re-settlement. And indeed a very large number of the people, of the men in the camps, did sign these forms, and then they were taken out of the camp, back to their original home. They were given between a few minutes and a few hours to collect their belongings, family members, and then taken to the border between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, where they were met by the Croatian police and escorted in this case to the Obonjan refugee camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we turn momentarily to the question of humanitarian convoys, and I guess at this point just to confirm again that this was an issue that you and the United States government were raising with the Croatian and Bosnian Croat officials throughout this period.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Also the -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to clarify something. I seem to think, Mr. Ambassador, that you asked for authorisation for the people working for the embassy to be able to go to the Heliodrom. Now, did you in fact send someone to Heliodrom, people cooperating with your embassy, embassy staff, or whoever, or didn't they see those localities except when they were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They -- I sent embassy staff to the Heliodrom, and they went into the Heliodrom and they filed a report on what they found in the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We have a specific document reporting that, Your Honour, that we're coming to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To touch on the other -- one of the other issues you've mentioned, sir, were you also continuing to raise throughout this time issuing concerning the siege and the shelling of east Mostar?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before we look at some of these additional documents that we're going to get to, going back to the relationship between the HV and the HVO, that is the Croatian army and the Herceg-Bosna army, had you specifically raised with Tudjman and others by this point the issue of the HV's involvement in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And by this time was this -- again, was this an issue uniquely known and raised by you or was this something that was a matter that again generally being discussed and raised by the international community?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was generally known by the international community. I cannot speak to how much my diplomatic colleagues may have raised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any understanding at this time -- Mr. Praljak has come up a couple of times in your testimony so far. As an example, did you know what Mr. Praljak's position had been in the Croatian government or army before coming to Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, as I recall, he held a senior position and had been a general in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, whether there was any discussion in the international -- perhaps in the embassy or in the international community at that time -- I don't -- I'm asking you, I don't know if it was said literally or figuratively, that the HB and the HVO insignia patches were attached with Velcro, could be changed one to the other?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: We certainly discussed that in the embassy, and I think it was literally true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I raise with you the knowledge of this issue in the international community. Can I ask you, please, to be shown Exhibit P05047?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a question of information. I'm not sure I know what Velcro stands for. I can imagine, but I'm -- I would like to know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I should answer you or the witness should answer you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For anybody, if you have small children you know, it is the -- it is a sticky material that attaches two pieces of fabric together. So children who no longer have to tie their shoelaces, they have Velcro on their shoes, they fold over the flap, and it seals it, but of course it can also be for patches that you can take off your patch and change your patch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I now know it's also referred to in my language, at least, as a strip-tease attachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I was asking the usher to show you Exhibit P05047, and if we could enlarge the English portion, please. Sir, do you recall generally around this time, you may or may not recall this particular item, but that again the issue of Croatia's -- the involvement of Croatia and its armed forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and specifically in the conflict with the Muslims was being raised in the international community, including the UN Security Council?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Of course this was being raised by the international community, as evidenced by this presidential statement of the Security Council. And the United States as a permanent member of the Security Council would have been one of the -- either the sponsors of supporters of this statement. So this statement reflected the views of the -- views and concerns of the United States government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And at the end of this -- this specifically talks about the camps, among other issues, but I think in particular the camps. The last paragraph, did that again make this connection or linkage of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is a statement that Croatia is responsible for what the Bosnian Croats are doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think perhaps the gentleman should look at the last paragraph again. I mean, it talks about a responsibility to use influence. Now, how you get to responsible for actions, I think it's a bit of a stretch. I understand the gentleman wishes to help the Prosecution, but let's have some balance here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I object to the attack on the witness, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's no attack on the witness. I'm pointing the obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said he's anxious to help the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me explain a statement like this, what this means from translating from diplomatic language into plain English. The -- when the Security Council calls on a government and says that it has a responsibility to use its influence, this is, in fact, a -- with a -- with a supposed foreign party and calls on that government to take immediate steps to that end, this is an incredibly strong statement. If the Security Council did not believe that -- that Croatia was responsible, the statement would have been directed solely Bosnian Croat political authorities, who after all ostensibly were from another country. It is precisely because this kind of formulation reflects precisely the belief of the United States government, but frankly a belief that was shared by other members of the Security Council, that Croatia was responsible for the conduct of the Bosnian Croats and that it was upon Croatia -- the responsibility of Croatia to take immediate action.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, there's one topic I want to raise with you briefly. Did it come to your attention around this time - and if so, I'll ask you how - that there was -- supposedly had been some letter from the British Prime Minister John Major to the British official Hogg that was circulating in the Tudjman -- Croatian presidential offices?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How did that come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: As I recall, President Tudjman asked me to come up and see him and showed me the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you see the letter?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did see the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was your conclusion upon looking at it?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was an obvious forgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you communicate that to President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What were some of the reasons that made it obvious to you that it was a false or forged document?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was highly improbable that the British Prime Minister would have written to a subordinate minister a letter outlining his views in that way, and the views were -- were not plausible -- were not plausible ones that the British Prime Minister likely would have had and certainly not ones that he would have put down on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall whether they were also grammatical and other errors in the English that was used?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: If I saw the letter again, I would -- I suspect that was the case. I don't recall now actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: But I -- it was very clear to me that it was a forgery for all sorts of reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you immediately in this meeting pointed that out to President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to next go to -- excuse me. Exhibit P06251.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I say that, I look at the clock. I'm about to start a new document. I don't know if the Chamber wants to take the break now or to go for a while longer. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you wish. It's 20 minutes past 12.00. We'll take our 20-minute break and re-convene in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, you have the floor until a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We were about to go to P06251, please. Sir, this is a record of a meeting at the presidential palace on the 29th of October, 1993. It indicates that two of the persons present at the meeting were a Timothy E. Wirth and apparently yourself, Mr. Galbraith. Can you tell the Judges who Mr. Wirth was, what position he held, and why he was there?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He was the counselor for the state department, with responsibility for global issues including refugee matters. He was a former senator from Colorado and he was there to deal with the -- to look at the refugee issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention, please, to page 6. The paragraph on the page starting with the words "I spoke recently ..." I think the record will show this is President Tudjman speaking. And the second -- sorry, the third sentence beginning: "There are even some proposals to allow that Serbian republic from Bosnia to join Serbia immediately, while only the Muslim and Croat republics would remain in the union. This standpoint is not acceptable for Croatia because Croats would be in the minority in such a union, but we would be in favour of this (as printed). We are in favour of the union being retained and of the Bosnian, Muslim, and Croatian republics being bound together as firmly as possible within the union. If the situation is already such that the Serbs would join Serbia, to which Izetbegovic has agreed in his agreement with the Serbs, then the Croat republic should join Croatia, but the Muslim republic should be bound by a treaty on friendship, on a common defence, into a firmer alliance with Croatia." Now, can we stop there, sir, and, Mr. Ambassador, is this essentially a continuation of the same types of conversations that we looked at earlier with President Tudjman about how to reorganisation Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and what's important here is that he sees a new influential American envoy and so he's hoping to make the case to Counselor Wirth, and of course is also misrepresenting the position of the ambassadors of Germany and France.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you say that, you're making references to the opening part of the paragraph: "I spoke recently with the ambassadors of Germany and France."

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yeah, it seems no one in Europe believes any longer that the union of Bosnia-Herzegovina can be maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you knew that not to be the case?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to continue over to page 10 where Mr. Wirth then speaks. Several lines down Mr. Wirth says: "As Ambassador Zimmermann said during his talks with you two weeks ago, we are still very concerned about aid deliveries to refugees in Bosnia. We know that you are trying to influence the HVO and you do have certain influence in other matters and, as you know, this is very difficult, but we appreciate your efforts and assume that we are doing everything" -- sorry. "We assure you that we are doing everything in our power to assist in the efforts of the international community to ensure aid. We hope that the aid will reach its destination. However, unless there is a cessation of hostilities, we will be unable to deliver the aid. I wouldn't be completely honest if I didn't tell you that some circles in our administration are dissatisfied with the activities of the HVO, that is, the stopping of aid, and some are even saying that perhaps additional sanctions should be introduced to exert more pressure on you so that you increase pressure on the HVO." Now, a couple of questions. There's a reference here to Ambassador Zimmermann. Can you tell us or at least remind us perhaps of who Ambassador Zimmermann was at this time and what his role in these matters was.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He was the Assistant Secretary of State for refugee and migration issues, and therefore directly responsible for refugee issues, actually reporting to the Secretary of State through counselor Wirth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And according it this record, in fact, Ambassador Zimmermann had met with President Tudjman in the past approximately two weeks. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I was not in Zagreb when that meeting took place or it's also possible, actually, that the meeting was not in Zagreb but someplace else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, is this a further example of in this instance of Mr. Wirth being the messenger, that again if you don't take -- do everything possible to correct the conduct of the HVO, there could be sanctions against Croatia itself?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, that was the message that he was delivering.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then changing topics from humanitarian aid to Stupni Do, in the next paragraph it says: "Finally, I must mention that the United States was truly shocked by the recent discovery, two days ago, and thus it would be useful that you condemned it as soon as possible, bringing those responsible" - next page - "to justice as soon as possible." Did the atrocities and massacre committed at Stupni Do come to your attention around this time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And going on that same page, did you yourself raise and protest what had happened at Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I -- in fact, I had instructions to make a demarche to Tudjman on the matter, and so I gave him a copy of the demarche, but spoke to him about the impact that Stupni Do had had on the Clinton administration, as well as the American public.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in your intervention on page 11, the second line of that -- the second sentence of that confirms, indeed, as you said, you had delivered a copy of the demarche?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, I may have missed something. How do we know this refers to Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, for example, the second -- the sentence we just read, Mr. Galbraith: "In connection with this, let me just add, Mr. President, that I received instructions today to specifically raise the issue of the massacre in Stupni Do."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going on over to page 12 then, again there's additional talk about humanitarian convoys and the camps again -- no, I'm sorry, convoys -- no, I was right the first time, camps and convoys. And then Tudjman starts speaking and he says after referring to Mr. Wirth: "We were truly appalled by what happened two days ago." Do you see that on page 12?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- was this the only time that you or the United States government raised Stupni Do or was this something that was at least around the end of October and into November 1993, this was something that was raised as a very serious issue on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, to deliver a demarche on the matter to the -- the head of state and who is also de facto the head of government of the country to which you're accredited is as strong an expression of concern as you can have. But I'm also sure that I raised this with -- in discussions with Granic and with Susak and with others in the course of my diplomatic dealings with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps it's a very basic point. It may be that most people in the court-room know this, but I suppose for the record, purposes of the record, in diplomatic terminology when something is called or described as a demarche, what is that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Well, a demarche is a message from a -- a formal message from one government to another. It can be a communication of views or a set of demands or warnings. And in this case this was certainly an -- a formal expression of our great concern about Stupni Do, a statement that it was unacceptable, and most certainly a warning of the consequences of this kind of behaviour that they would have for Croatia. Basically, a demarche is a series of talking points that would be presented orally, but the normal practice, certainly my practice, then would be to hand over the piece of paper so that the government would understand word for word what the message that had been delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me go back to page 11. With the assistance of the usher, please. In your intervention, we can scroll down the page you say: "People were shocked when they saw photographs of what happened. This was obviously done by Bosnian Croats. We pointed out several times that since you support the HVO we would hold you responsible for its activities." And my question to you is: During this conversation with President Tudjman, was there any denial the allegation or your statement that Stupni Do had been carried out by the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: So far as I recall, no. What Tudjman did say, which was characteristic, was that the Bosnian -- that the Bosnian Muslims had done something bad the previous week. But there was not a denial so far as I recall of the Bosnian Croats having committed the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then continuing back -- we can go back to the bottom of page 12, carrying over to page 13, in fact Tudjman concludes this particular topic, the bottom of that page: "I, the Croatian government, our deputy minister, and the minister of foreign affairs, Granic, as stated here, issued a statement about this that we condemn these crimes and demand that the perpetrators be punished. We shall exert our full influence to prevent such acts." Do you recall whether the United States government, through you or otherwise, if you recall, received any sort of follow-up information, whether in fact any HVO officer or soldier had been punished or prosecuted for the crime committed at Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: At this stage, I do not recall definitively, but I do not believe there was any prosecution for the crimes committed at Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can then turn to -- for the Ambassador and the court-room, what we're going to do now is go through an additional documents and cables, touching on a number of things that the Ambassador has mentioned this morning. The first one if Exhibit P09502.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is this a cable, sir, dated the 5th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: From the Zagreb embassy reporting to Washington?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you made reference earlier today to one of the missions you had sent to the Croatian refugee camp where Muslim men who had been released from the HVO camps had been sent and then were interviewed. And in looking at this document, sir, can you tell the Judges, is this a cable describing the work and the report of this mission?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is right. It's a report -- a consolidated report of the teams that -- of embassy officers, that's what the phrase EMBOFs means, that went to Obonjan island July 24th, 25th, and also the team that visited the refugee centre at Gasinci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The introduction and summary provides a fairly detailed summary, as you know, of this seven -- perhaps seven- or eight-page report. Looking at item number 2, paragraph number 2, under the heading of: "Rounding up Muslims," do you see this line which: "Beginning on the night of June 30, uniformed HVO troops and military police on the Croatian-controlled west bank of the Neretva river in Mostar began searching door to door for Muslim males." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is this an example of the information that was being obtained from the men who were being -- who had been interviewed in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in paragraph 5 on the next page there's quite a bit of information in these documents, but again we won't have time to go through every detail. On paragraph number 5 do you recall it being reported -- one of the things being reported was the practice of forced labour on the Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you recall anything more about that or was this only reported on this one occasion or is this something that was continuing to come to your attention during this time period?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was a continual feature of the way in which detainees were abused in the Muslim-Croat war. But specifically these forced labour parties occurred on a daily basis at the Heliodrom. They were deployed often to the front lines where they were then exposed to fire from Bosnian government troops who were -- and the front lines were very close. So it exposed the prisoners to not only forced labour but great personal risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is also a report in paragraph 8 of not only what was happening to the detained Muslim men but the families that were still in Mostar. If you see that.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Reports about rapes and murders. If we can continue on over to paragraph 11 on the next page. The heading titled: "Third country re-settlement." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if you look at this paragraph 11, sir, you get a fairly detailed confirmation, I believe, of what you told the Judges earlier this morning. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: No, it -- to restate it is that the HVO authorities offered to release prisoners who signed a request for assistance and retaining re-settlementing to a third country. The reports we had that were about half the men in the Heliodrom signed up and filled out a questionnaire with the desired country of destination. On July 17, buses took the men who had signed to Mostar, where they were ordered to collect their families and report back. Some were given 30 minutes, others three hours to gather their relatives. During the night of July 17/18, eight buses transported over 800 people to the Obonjan refugee centre. The process was repeated on July 20th, when 180 more went to the island. A second convoy of ten buses took several hundred to the Gasinci centre on July 20th. Then just to note the next paragraph is -- confirms what I said, which is that the Croatian police were waiting at the border for the convoys to arrive and escorted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think for purposes of concluding with this document, of course unless some -- unless the Judges have questions, if we could go to paragraph 28 on the next-to-last page. In the context of talking again about labour work details, in that same paragraph it says: "They spent the entire day building bunkers near the 'management building' for mortars operated by soldiers in Croatian army (HV) uniforms. He said soldiers and HVO uniforms were also at the airport, but they were some distance away near the air strip. On the way back to the Heliodrom he said he saw a tank with a Croatian army (HV) insignia." Is that the kind of information that would be reported back to you and to the embassy and others from time to time?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could next go to Exhibit P09503.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just briefly, Ambassador, this is a cable dated the 6th of August, 1993, and by way of balance was information coming to the US embassy in Zagreb from time to time about situations on which Croats were victims of alleged misconduct or war -- what might be called war crimes?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we devoted considerable effort to collecting information about all war crimes that took place in Bosnia, and these included Croat victims of Serbian aggression as well as Croat victims of Bosnian government attacks in the Muslim-Croat war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you next please to go to P09504.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, is this a cable dated the 10th of August, 1993, reporting on the second of the two missions that you described earlier today, this one being to the Heliodrom facility itself?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was that mission sent by you or under your supervision?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was sent by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Bottom of the first page: "The commander, who never gave his name, stated that there were some 1400 prisoners in the facility and that at no time in the last month were there more than 2.000. He evaded questions about how many people had passed through the facility during that period and was unable to say how long the present group of detainees would remain." Do you recall who in the embassy was in particular most directly involved, if you will, if he was maybe the senior member of the team or -- who reported this to you?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you please just give us that information?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It was Tom Mitnacht.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This report reinforced the concerns which you've expressed today about what was happening in the HVO camps?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going to the last page, which says: "Overall assessment." Was one of the particular issues that was being raised during this time was not only the fact of the camps and the conditions of the camps but whether international organisations had been allowed access?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, that was very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this report -- the second sentence on -- under "overall assessment": The continued interference with ICRC visits is inexplicable and intolerable and the camp leaders were so informed." Ambassador, is this the sort of thing that following the receipt of this information this is something that you would have raised again with Tudjman, Susak, and others?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly would have raised it with the senior officials in the Croatian government. I'm sure I raised this with Mate -- this specific issue with Mate Granic, and it would be part of the -- of the key issues that I would raise with Tudjman and Susak, these kinds of concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going to Exhibit then P09505, a cable dated the 24th of August, 1993. It's a short document, again talks about the delivery of a demarche to President Tudjman on the morning of August 24th. Do you recall anything more about the subject of this particular demarche or conversation?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Certainly the broad subject of the demarche was the HVO's conduct in blocking humanitarian assistance and humanitarian access to the Bosniak population in Mostar and -- and the -- and likely other issues, including the shelling of east Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your -- I'm sorry. I didn't mean to interrupt you. Directing your attention to the last sentence. Is it correct, sir, that you reported that: "The ambassador said that there was no excuse for starving the Muslim civilian population, that two wrongs don't make a right. President Tudjman agreed."

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is true that I said that and it is true that he agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection, sir, this cable was sent on the 24th of August. Do you have any recollection, sir, of the efforts to get humanitarian convoys into the Mostar region as of the end of August 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I -- following this cable -- sorry, following in demarche, convoys then went into Mostar. I think it's very important to understand here that -- first that this was a very tough warning to Tudjman that we delivered, and he did not deny what was going on. He in fact asserted responsibility in saying that he would use all of his influence to accept such a reasonable appeal, the reasonable appeal being for the access of humanitarian assistance. "I will do all that I can do." He -- although he then of course tried to raise other issues. He readily agreed that there was no excuse for the starving of the Muslim population, and subsequently to this, very promptly he did take action.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think there's a question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to ask you, Mr. Galbraith, about your very last sentence when he -- when you said and he quoted -- and I quote you that: "He readily agreed that there was no excuse for starving the Muslim population and subsequent to this very probably he did take action." I wonder if you would be able to tell us a little bit more about what happened after that, what your last sentence suggested. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within a few days, convoys did have access to east Mostar and humanitarian supplies were delivered. I think it's an important point that this was a case where our diplomatic interventions produced results, and it is in that sense somewhat different from the experience of the United Nations and also, frankly, the experience in dealing with the Milosevic government where demarches and interventions would fall on deaf ears, on denials, on promises to do something and then nothing would happen. Here, actually, things did happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we can then in fact go on to Exhibit P09506, two days later. Can you tell us, Ambassador, is this a cable from the US embassy in Zagreb to -- excuse me, dated the 31st of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you speak to Susak, the defence minister, the Croatian defence minister, around this time about continuing concerns that you had?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that basically reporting -- in part what this cable is about, reporting your conversation with Susak?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Partly as well as a call I had from an individual in east Mostar, which in turn led me to go see Susak and to demand that the HVO shelling of east Mostar stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ambassador, the -- the Chamber has heard evidence concerning a time when a Spanish Battalion force that accompanied a convoy into east Mostar at this time was held or detained, if you will, or presented from leaving east Mostar around this time, the end of August 1993. Now, directing your attention to the second part of your report where it says: "Also reported ..." I take it this information had come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "UN forces trapped in east Mostar would be permitted to leave as soon as the officials of east Mostar were in radio contact with a replacement force." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I had been told by a -- what I'm -- a UN official who was in east Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going further down the page you also say that: "The Ambassador raised the issue of the shelling of east Mostar with Defence Minister Susak at a previously arranged lunch meeting." And if you look at this, and I'll just ask you to tell the Judges, what was Susak's response when you raised this issue with him?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: He promised that -- Susak promised he would be immediately in contact with HVO Commander Praljak to demand a stop to the shelling. He then went on to complain about the lack of discipline in the HVO and the inability to halt a range of abuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can go on to Exhibit P0950 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask a follow-up question at this point. In the telegram it says that Mr. Susak indicated that he would contact Mr. Praljak in order to stop the bombing. Were you certain that there was a link between Mr. Susak and Mr. Praljak and between Mr. Praljak and the bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Although this is probably a matter for cross-examination, I think that we clearly heard here from the gentleman from Spanish Bat, that while they were detained there was absolutely no shelling in Mostar whatsoever. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you could have put that question during the cross-examination because you are interrupting the examination-in-chief. Yes, we have another question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you mentioned during your testimony the links that existed between Zagreb and the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in this same telegram I can see that it says: Mr. Susak who is complaining about the lack of discipline among the HVO ranks. Now, what are your comments, what do you think about that? Was it an actual lack of discipline and the fact that the link between Zagreb and the HVO was not at a high level or was that just an excuse on his part, if you understand my meaning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly understand your question. The -- his statement to me was about the lack of discipline of HVO soldiers and perhaps more junior officers in terms of following the orders that were being given from Zagreb through the -- through the HVO command down to the field. That was what he was -- he was saying to me. His statement at that lunch and at every other occasion where this issue came up, but his statement at that lunch was that he had -- was that he would demand a halt to the shelling and that he had the power to demand such a halt because he was, in effect, not only the defence minister for the Republic of Croatia, but also the defence minister in charge of the HVO. And he never made any pretense that this was a separate entity, and I think that's clear -- that certainly was clear to me in that interaction and in every other interaction. As to where the lack of discipline took place in the HVO, that was much harder to pin down. On some occasions the suggestion was that it was at the case of individual soldiers or junior commanders. In other cases, the suggestion was that Praljak was undisciplined and not following instructions and that they were angry with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And a final question following on from what we've just heard. In your relationships and meetings with Mr. Susak, he told you that there were problems of discipline and you have told us that Mr. Susak had two posts he occupied. He was defence minister, but also the minister in charge of the HVO. So as an ambassador yourself and somebody who's well-versed in administrative posts and functions, didn't you perhaps ask him whether he was giving out his instructions in written form or over the phone. Did you ever discuss that because you spoke of the lack of discipline and he said he'd do what he could, and then something happened or didn't happen. But do you know how he sent out these instructions and what the information line between Zagreb and Mostar was, how this was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to clarify my testimony, I said that -- of course that he has the -- held the position -- the formal position of defence minister of Croatia and therefore had responsibility as the top civilian for the HV, the Croatian army. I also said that he had de facto responsibility for the HVO, but of course he didn't have a formal position. But in reality he was -- he functioned also as the defence minister in charge of the HVO. As to -- I don't -- I don't recall inquiring in great detail as to how he transmitted his orders because frankly I didn't want to get into that issue. It was, from my point of view, the best situation for him to take responsibility and for me, therefore, to say: Either this happens or there are consequences. We hold you responsible. I didn't want to raise any -- go into any chain of command issues. He took responsibility. As far as I was concerned, if the HVO continued with these atrocities, I could hold Susak responsible, I could hold the Croatian government responsible, and the United States government could act on that basis and we were not interested in hearing all the excuses. Now, I believe -- he was very close to the Bosnian Croat leadership, so I -- and I imagine that he -- whatever orders were submitted -- were transmitted in writing, there was also plenty of oral communication via telephone and in person. He also went down to the Croat areas of Bosnia; he was in fact from there, from Siroki Brijeg, and he was very proud of that area and often went home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could then go on to Exhibit P09507.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, can you confirm that this is a cable from the US embassy in Zagreb dated the 6th of September, yes?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The letter or the cable, excuse me, largely perhaps speaks for itself, but if you will want to confirm or elaborate on any of the points you made. It's fair to say that throughout this period you were, again, continuing on almost a daily basis to raise various issues with the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That is correct. And I think you can see from these cables that the tone of them which started out firm becomes even more insistent in terms of the demands that we made. And we -- I did not use a lot of diplomatic language. They were demands that we expected Zagreb to comply with, and the reason that we made these demands on Zagreb is that we were certain that they were responsible and that they could comply with our demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just as -- by way of connection to one of the earlier documents, on paragraph 3 you refer back to the mission that had been sent in a document about some of the problems in the camps. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Over a month ago we reported ..."

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: And you will note that I -- that it's pointed out in this cable that I've repeatedly raised this issue in numerous meetings with Foreign Minister Granic as well as with President Tudjman and -- and then I think it's perhaps worth noting the fourth paragraph which is that: "As he has in the past, Granic has promised further efforts of persuasion. We believe he is sincere and his work has had some limited success; however, we believe if the abuses are to end Croatia must take concrete actions against the HVO."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in that regard, then, if we continue over to the next page and specifically to item number 7. Do you see where it says that: "Granic said that President Tudjman, with whom he spoke September 5, was sending a formal letter to HVO leader Mate Boban September 6 to urge in the strongest possible terms that the Bosnian Croats respect and comply with international humanitarian law."

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again, at the paragraph -- at the end of paragraph 10 at the bottom of that page you once again stress as you did before that you and the US government expect results and not anything less than that?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: That's right. Again, reflecting our belief that Croatia was fully responsible for the actions of the HVO, and therefore capable of producing results. And therefore, good intentions or letters or demarches or persuasion or even public denunciations was not sufficient. The only thing that mattered was the results.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in the paragraph 7 that we were looking at just a moment ago says: "Tudjman is going to send a formal letter to Boban to urge compliance with international humanitarian law." Can I ask that you next be shown Exhibit P05104. If you can look at that document, sir. You may or may not have seen this document at the time. You can tell us whether you did or didn't, but can you see that in fact a few days later, on the 15th of September, 1993, according to this document in fact Mr. Boban did issue, as indicated would be requested by President Tudjman, an order or instruction that the HVO forces comply with international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going on to Exhibit P09508. Can you confirm, Mr. Ambassador, that this is a cable from the US embassy in Zagreb dated the 10th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you receive from Croatian government officials around this time, if you will, a progress report, admittedly that's my characterisation, but a further report on what was to be done with the camps?

utterances.speaker: PETER GALBRAITH
utterances.text: I was receiving constant updates and this is -- this cable reports on one of the more significant developments, which was that the HVO would close all but three detention camps and that the remaining camps would be open to daily visits by the ICRC and that Croatia would provide humanitarian assistance which would also monitor the conditions of the prisoners. Once again, a message on the camps delivered by the Croatian foreign minister to me, the American ambassador in Croatia, effectively taking -- demonstrating that his efforts had produced results, as we requested, and noting that, you know, formally that Croatia was taking additional responsibilities, including the monitoring of conditions. Incidentally, so far as I recall, there was virtually no interaction on the -- there was -- these -- the Bosnian Croat authorities were not dealing with the embassy -- American embassy in Sarajevo or there. I mean, all this was coming through Zagreb because this was where -- this was where the Bosnian Croats looked, and of course this is where Croatia took responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm glad you raised that because actually I was going to ask you that. We've focussed on the embassy in Zagreb and the dealings with the Croatian government. Were you receiving any information during this time from your colleague, the -- your -- the US ambassador that was situated in Bosnia at Sarajevo on these similar issues or was all this being channeled essentially through Zagreb?
